Suburbs originated with something called the Garden City movement emerging in the late 19th century. Partly a response to the impacts of urban industrialization earlier in the century that had made many large cities unlivable. The Garden City idea sought to use restrictions on density, an emphasis on residence over other activities, and the cultivation of intentional green spaces as a way of creating a healthier and more pleasant environment.

The typical American suburb was a product of the post-WWII building boom and was heavily influenced by planned housing developments following models such as Levittown developed in the period between the wars as automobile use expanded with the rapid expansion of the middle-class through New Deal economic evolution. Rapid post-war suburban development was pursued to address the housing crisis created as thousands of soldiers returned from the war, but the New Deal also brought with it a cultural model of the American Dream and middle-class status that was rooted in the idea of individual property ownership only possible in the suburbs --something that had been formerly quite rare and which remained so in most other western nations.

Mid-century, urban planners and real estate speculators began pursuing a vision of cities as predominantly commercial centers dominated by corporate HQs and began ejecting industry to the urban periphery. This inadvertently (or intentionally...) created slums from former middle-class residential areas whose decrepitude and rising crime encouraged increasing middle-class flight to the suburbs. We began to see distinctions between 'inner' and 'outer' urban areas and 'inner' and 'outer' suburbs defined largely by economic class.

But cities run on taxes, and driving away the middle-class left cities impoverished as corporations never pay their fair share. Bad urban economic management in the '70s, exacerbated by economic contraction resulting from the Energy Crisis triggered a wave of urban decay across the major cities of the US. Slum growth worsened and urban flight was accelerated and with middle-class people becoming commuters and the suburbs becoming vast, amorphous, 'bedroom communities' whose primary purpose was to be a place to own property, sleep, and raise children. But they were increasingly 'placeless' and became oppressive in aspect, particularly for those children growing up in them. By the late 20th century commute distances had reached their limit and cities attempts to restore their tax bases, along with the advent of IT and advanced telecommunications, resulted in a wave of corporate flight to large campuses in the suburbs. And so emerged the idea of Edge Cities growing at the commute limits as corporate campuses and gigantic shopping malls became new nexuses of jobs and commerce. These, however, were precarious as the presence of corporate campuses depended on unsustainable tax deals with local municipalities.

By the end of the century retail went into a protracted decline, bringing the slow death of the mall, entrepreneurship empowered by IT returned to the cities, and a wave of re-urbanization and gentrification was catalyzed by the rise of a new young middle-class--yuppies--who sought a more cultured lifestyle than the suburbs could offer in traditional inner-urban residence areas renovated after their poorer inhabitants were driven to older inner-suburbs. Thus we come to the present where restored urban residential areas are dominated by the upper-middle-class, inner-suburbs are now the province of the poor, mainstream outer-suburbs are now dominated by the lower-middle-class, and the periphery a mix of enclaves for the rich and the white rural underclass. With the real estate crash of 2008 and the rise of automation this has all been thrown into a state of flux whose resulting form is still up-for-grabs with the emergence of a new middle-class-precariat.
